task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of January 14, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Redcliff Tunnel — a proposed 4.2-kilometer road tunnel beneath a urban neighborhood — has been in environmental review for 11 years and its final approval decision is expected in spring 2025.

Civil engineer Marcus Oduya, 58, led the project's original planning team and retired in 2022 before a decision was made; he is now a transportation consultant who says the project's delay has been professionally formative.
Oduya said: "I designed that tunnel to solve a traffic problem that existed in 2013. I can't tell you whether it solves the 2025 problem because we haven't made decisions fast enough to find out."
The delay cost an estimated $280 million in inflation-adjusted construction cost increases; the project is now projected to cost $1.4 billion, up from $840 million in the 2013 estimate.

Key points of contention: an underground aquifer that an early environmental study underestimated, community opposition from the Ridgemont neighborhood over surface disruption during construction, and two competing surface alternatives proposed by environmental advocates.

Ridgemont resident Carmen Osei, 43, leads the Ridgemont Traffic Justice Coalition, which opposed the tunnel in its current form but says the coalition is not anti-tunnel in principle — it wants a rerouted alignment that avoids the neighborhood's historic district.
Osei said: "We were told in 2016 that they had heard our concerns. We were told in 2019 that they had heard our concerns. We are still here in 2025."

An independent review commissioned by the state in 2023 found the aquifer management plan inadequate for the project's depth profile in its northeastern section; the plan was revised but critics say the revision is also inadequate.
Traffic on the surface arterials that the tunnel is meant to relieve has continued to grow; the corridor now handles 92,000 vehicle trips per day, compared to 71,000 in the original planning study.

Transportation planner Veronica Cheng, who advises the city on the alternative surface options, said: "A transit-oriented surface redesign could absorb a third of those trips and cost a fifth as much. But it requires taking roadway space away from cars, and that is politically very hard."
The state transportation department has publicly committed to a decision by June 2025; a department spokesperson said a decision will not be delayed again.
Federal highway funds for the project expire in September 2025; losing the $620 million federal commitment would require the state to restart the funding process.
Oduya said he visits the project's staging area occasionally: "It's a hole in the ground and a billboard. Eleven years. The city is holding its breath."
Community surveys conducted in 2024 found 58% of Ridgemont residents prefer the rerouted alignment to the original, but 61% of city-wide respondents prefer the faster original alignment.
Three council members have publicly called for a full project restart; two others have said cancellation would waste the $340 million already spent on design and permitting.

Cheng said the delay has itself changed the problem: transit ridership in the corridor has grown 40% since 2013, meaning the case for a transit alternative is now stronger than when the tunnel was first proposed.
The project's prime contractor has maintained a standby contract at an annual cost of $12 million since 2021, awaiting a decision to proceed.

Osei said her coalition will go to court if the original alignment is approved without addressing the historic district concerns; a previous lawsuit by the coalition was dismissed on procedural grounds.
Oduya said he hopes for a decision, whatever it is: "A bad decision we can learn from. No decision is just time and money and opportunity disappearing."
The state has not disclosed which alignment it prefers; the transportation director said the decision will incorporate community feedback, traffic modeling, and cost.
